It was a pleasure to connect at this year’s IAPP Global Summit! The privacy world does not pause for conference week, however, and there were some big news items. The Seventh Circuit held that the 2024 BIPA amendment on claim accrual applies retroactively to claims pending at the time the amendment was signed. Maine’s comprehensive privacy bill has stalled after the House failed a vote to enact. The FTC announced a settlement concerning sharing of personal data with a third party not disclosed in the company’s privacy notice. 🟢 Reflections from IAPP Global Summit: It was a pleasure connecting with members at this year’s IAPP Global Summit. Here are a few of the team’s takeaways from panels and events this week:

  • The “Future of Youth Personalization” panel discussed the growing global scrutiny of personalization in youth digital experiences. Key takeaways from panelists include: services should be built for youth (rather than from youth); developmental psychologists and researchers should be part of the conversation; responsive regulations or mitigations should be risk-proportionate and informed by reliable research; and more research to inform evidence-based public policy for regulating personalized digital experiences is critically necessary.
  • The “Less is More” panel discussed data minimization’s role in privacy laws, leaning on the “procedural” and “substantive” framing from FPF’s data minimization white paper. Panelists highlighted the importance of explicitly addressing processing activities that policymakers want to either prohibit or allow, practicing data minimization in the context of complying with consumers rights requests, and potential issues with enforcing data minimization violations.
  • The “State Collaboration on Privacy” panel featured representatives from CalPrivacy and the attorney general offices of California, Connecticut, Delaware, and Indiana. The panelists discussed: how they coordinate on investigations and enforcement, including through the bipartisan Consortium of Privacy Regulators; the importance for business's to cooperate with their office during an investigation or inquiry to quickly resolve the matter; how remediating conduct during an investigation can reduce penalties; how penalties for violations may increase going forward; and enforcement priorities, such as connected TVs and similar devices, OOPS, “surveillance pricing,” dark patterns, and chatbots interacting with kids. Several panelists discussed shifting enforcement strategies from facial violations and “low hanging fruit” towards more difficult questions around data use and how companies are operationalizing data flows.

 

💬 New Resource on Utah ASAA Amendment: Utah amended its App Store Accountability Act earlier this month when Governor Cox signed HB 498. This bill narrows the “significant changes” definition, adds new age verification and parental consent requirements for pre-installed apps and existing accounts, and clarifies that developers are not prohibited from allowing a parent to customize age-related restrictions, safety features, and settings from mandatory defaults in minor accounts. See FPF’s updated analysis of the law here.

 

💬 New Resource - Chatbot Law Comparison Chart: FPF has released a new comparison chart analyzing the three West Coast chatbot laws: newly signed Oregon’s SB 1546 and Washington’s HB 2225, as well as California’s SB 243 from last year. The chart highlights key differences in scope, requirements, and enforcement across these frameworks as states continue to shape companion chatbot regulation.

 

Stuff from the States 

 

Illinois - Seventh Circuit Rules BIPA Claim Accrual Amendment Applies Retroactively: Claim accrual is a longstanding issue under BIPA. The Supreme Court of Illinois ruled in 2023 that a separate claim for a statutory damages accrues under the Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) each time a private entity scans or transmits an individual’s biometric identifier or information without prior informed consent. The Illinois legislature amended the law in 2024 to clarify that a private entity that repeatedly collects or discloses a person's biometric identifier or biometric information from the same person in violation of the Act has committed a single violation for which the aggrieved person is entitled to one recovery, effectively overturning the White Castle decision. This week, the Seventh Circuit held that the amendment applies retroactively to cases that were pending at the time the amendment was enacted. The court applied the Illinois law of retroactivity and determined that the amendment was a remedial (i.e., procedural) change to the law because it “addresses the availability of damages, not proscribed conduct.” 

 

Kentucky - Smart TV Amendment PASSED LEGISLATURE (HB 692): An amendment to Kentucky’s comprehensive privacy law has been sent to the governor to be signed or vetoed. This bill would amend the KCDPA to prohibit a controller from collecting “automatic content recognition data” (captured by a smart television or smart monitor) without consent. The bill was amended to add exceptions, including for data “generated in the course of providing a feature or service requested by a consumer.”

 

Louisiana - Comprehensive Privacy Bill Passed Committee (SB 386): A Virginia-style comprehensive privacy bill was reported out of committee with amendments on April 1. Changes to the bill include replacing the applicability thresholds (now either $25 million in annual gross revenue; annually buying, receiving, selling, or sharing at least 75 thousand consumers’ personal information annually; or deriving 50% or more of annual revenue from personal), adding a general security/fraud exception, re-writing the attorney general enforcement provisions, and removing the private right of action. The bill is scheduled for floor action on April 7.

 

Maine - House FAILS Vote to Enact Comprehensive Privacy Bill (LD 1822): Maine’s comprehensive privacy bill has stalled late. The bill looked likely to pass after the Senate concurred with House amendments on March 30. The bill required an additional vote to enact, however, and that vote failed (68-80) as did the motion to reconsider (70-78) late Thursday night. The floor debate focused heavily on whether the Maryland-style data minimization provisions would restrict advertising, including for local businesses not within scope of the bill but who rely on advertising facilitated by larger companies. 

 

Ohio - Bill Banning Sale of Sensitive Data Introduced (HB 807): This bill would prohibit a state agency, state official, data broker, or private entity from selling, communicating, or otherwise furnishing sensitive data to any data broker or private entity “with the intent of generating profit from that data,” unless: the data will be used for a “permitted use”; the data is shared with the individual's informed consent; the data sharing is subject to a warrant, court order, or subpoena; or the data sharing is “otherwise required by state or federal law.” Sensitive data broadly “includes any information regarding an individual's name, date of birth, social security number, telephone number, character, general reputation, personal characteristics, immigration status, facial recognition data, or mode of living.” The bill includes a private right of action. 

 

Oregon - Data Broker Bill SIGNED (SB 1587): Governor Kotek signed SB 1587 into law on March 31. This law will prohibit a public body from disclosing personally identifiable information to a data broker unless the data broker first provides a written attestation that the information will not be sold or otherwise transferred to any entity that will use the information to enforce federal immigration law. 

 

Utah - ASAA Amendments ENACTED (HB 498): Governor Cox signed this bill into law on March 18. This amendment modifies Utah’s App Store Accountability Act (ASAA) to narrow the “significant changes” definition, add new age verification and parental consent requirements for pre-installed apps and existing accounts, and clarify that developers are not prohibited from allowing a parent to customize age-related restrictions, safety features, and settings from mandatory defaults in minor accounts. 

 

Federal Happenings

 

FTC Announces SETTLEMENT on Undisclosed Data Sharing: The Federal Trade Commission reached a settlement with dating app operator OkCupid, resolving allegations that the company deceived consumers in violation of Section 5 of the FTC Act. According to the complaint, the company allegedly shared users' personal information—including user photos, demographic data, and location data—with a third party in a manner that was not disclosed in the company’s privacy notice. Furthermore, the FTC alleged that the company did not offer users the opportunity to opt-out of the data sharing and concealed the arrangement after the fact. Although the complaint does not name the third party data recipient, Reuters reported that it was a facial recognition technology who used the shared data for training. That this was brought only as a deception claim and not an unfairness claim potentially highlights how the agency’s enforcement strategy has changed under Chair Ferguson’s leadership.
